Businesses using AI are far more optimistic about their growth:

Among US firms using AI, the share expecting revenue to increase over the next 12 months exceeds the share expecting a decrease by 48.2 percentage points, according to the Federal Reserve Banks' 2025 Small Business Credit Survey.

By comparison, this gap is just 20.6 percentage points among firms not using AI, less than half the figure for AI adopters.

At the same time, the share of AI-using firms expecting employment to increase exceeds the share expecting a decrease by 32.7 percentage points, compared to just 15.2 percentage points among non-adopters.

These differences persist even after accounting for firm characteristics, business-owner demographics, and changes in revenue and employment over the previous 12 months.

After adjusting for these factors, the gap between firms expecting revenue growth and those expecting a decline remains 14 percentage points wider among AI adopters than non-adopters.

For employment expectations, the corresponding gap remains 10 percentage points wider among AI adopters.

Businesses using AI are significantly more optimistic about their future expansion.

Energy stocks are making history:

The S&P 500 Energy sector took just 196 trading days to gain +50% year-to-date, marking the 5th-fastest time any S&P 500 sector has reached this milestone since 1990.

For perspective, in 2022, the Energy sector surged +50% in just 94 trading days, the fastest pace recorded over the last 36 years.

By comparison, the Technology sector reached the same milestone in 133 and 160 trading days in 1996 and 1997, respectively.

Consumer Discretionary, Consumer Staples, Industrials, Materials, and Real Estate have never recorded a +50% annual gain since 1990.

The Energy sector is witnessing one of its most remarkable rallies in decades.

China's automotive industry is facing a historic slowdown:

China’s automotive industry profit margin fell to 3.6% in the first 8 months of 2026, its lowest in at least 12 years.

This is now on track for its 12th consecutive annual decline.

Years of heavy investment have created severe production overcapacity, while weakening domestic demand is intensifying price wars among car manufacturers.

Meanwhile, in the first 8 months of 2026, domestic passenger vehicle sales dropped -22% YoY.

For the full year, car sales are expected to fall -22% YoY, to 18.5 million, their lowest annual total since 2014.

Now, factories have the capacity to produce a record ~62.9 million vehicles this year, more than 3 times the expected sales figure.

China’s auto industry is struggling.

The 35-40 and 31-34 cohorts have grown +11% and +6%, respectively.

As a result, the employment growth gap between the youngest and the oldest group has risen to 40 percentage points.

The AI boom is destroying job opportunities for entry-level tech workers.

BREAKING: US existing home sales dropped -5.5% MoM in October, to an annualized rate of 3.75 million, the lowest since August 2010.

Excluding the 2010 decline, this marks the lowest level since 1995.

YoY, existing home sales fell -8.8%, the largest annual decline since November 2023.

In the West, sales plunged -9.7% MoM last month, to an annualized rate of 650,000, the lowest since 1999.

Meanwhile, existing single-family home sales fell -5.8% MoM in October, to an annualized rate of 3.41 million, the lowest since October 2010.

This comes as 30Y mortgage rates surged to 7.6% last month, their highest level since 2000, excluding one month in 2023.

US housing demand is collapsing.

tweets.text: Coverage of gold ETFs in the media from 2014 to 2018 was absolutely brutal - as bad or worse than bitcoin lately - it was like a string of Morrissey song titles: 'new milestones in misery' 'massive disappointment' 'give up hope' 'a pet rock' and how it 'doesn't work' as safe haven or inflation hedge (tbf it did go down and stay down despite $5T in new money printed by gov). IMO notable for a few reasons. One, the disrespect came despite GLD 10x-ing SPX from 2004 to 2011 and was STILL beating it since 2004 ETF launch. Two, it proceeded to go up 250% over next 7yrs (easily beating bull mkt mode SPX) and Three, it had fallen to about $1200 an ounce, which would seem like a shockingly high number to anyone from distant past. Bigger takeaway here (and one that we point in the new book) is that assets without cash flows can be really hard to hold bc sentiment runs the show and they tend to do opposite of what you think/want and they get sht on the most from the media and high priests of investing despite how far they've come over long-term. It is a hard, hard road for investors. This was one of the reasons i was fascinated enough to write book on the topic.

No one was happier to see this week end than Nvidia $NVDA shareholders. Heading into Friday afternoon trading, the stock was down 14% this week and trading at its lowest levels since last summer. News of former CEO Jensen Huang’s multiple affairs hasn’t been kind to the stock, but if you look at the chart, most of its roughly 40% peak-to-trough decline since early October came before Huang admitted to the affairs last weekend. You could argue that the scandal started to show up in the stock price before the headlines did (as often happens), but Nvidia was also dealing with other issues besides who Huang was sleeping with, including a broad chip-sector selloff and growing worries about how the AI buildout will be financed.

￼This was NVDA’s sixth straight down week, and over its entire history as a public company, that’s tied with three other periods for the second-longest losing streak on record. The longest streak of weekly declines lasted seven weeks and ended in July 2008.

￼NVDA’s 14% decline this week doesn’t even rank as the worst week for the stock in the AI age that kicked off in late 2022. Where the week’s decline does stand out, though, is how poorly it performed relative to the S&P 500. With the S&P 500 up just over 2% this week, NVDA was poised to underperform the index by over 16 percentage points, which would rank as the weakest relative performance since November 2018, and before that you have to go back to 2009.

NVDA is hardly the first large-cap stock to fall 40%, even if you account for how quickly it declined. What is notable about the company, however, is how invested its 42,000 employees are in the stock. In 2008, Jensen Huang established an employee stock purchase plan (ESPP) that gave employees the option to purchase stock at a discount to the stock’s lowest price in the prior two years.

￼As the market recovered from the financial crisis lows and the stock price rallied, it created a massive incentive for employees to max out the ESPP. By January 2010, for example, the stock had rallied more than 200% off its November 2008 low. With employees owning so much stock and the stock outperforming almost every other publicly traded company, employees at the company got rich. According to an article on Yahoo! Finance back in May, “roughly 50% of employees now have a net worth exceeding $25 million.” That share is obviously lower now, but employees are still doing very well.

The question for the company is how the employees will react. Long-tenured employees have taken a big hit to their wealth but are still sitting on massive gains. The turmoil and change of leadership at the company, coupled with loyalty to Jensen Huang, could cause some to simply retire and take a step back from the grueling schedule at the company. Where things will become more interesting is among less-tenured employees. Many joined during the AI boom and received stock grants at far higher prices, so they don’t have the same cushion of gains.

According to an Inc. article, Nvidia’s employee turnover rate was 3.7% versus a tech industry average of 21.9%. Nvidia may be the happiest place on earth, but a big reason for the low turnover rate was that the company was doing so well. Employees had a financial incentive to stay not only for the prospect of future gains but also for the richly valued unvested shares. The lower stock price at least partially erases one factor keeping them at the company, and the prospect of increased regulatory and political pressure on the company could cause an increase in turnover among the ranks of the less-tenured employees. Will they look for greener and less cloudy pastures or will they choose to stick it out?

When Nvidia reports earnings next week, investors will be focused on sales and guidance. But the more telling number over the next few quarters may be how many employees decide the stock is no longer a strong enough glue to keep them in place.

Contrarians like to keep an eye on what major media outlets are saying. The reason isn't that they're ahead of the curve; it's usually the opposite. The basic assumption is that by the time something is major news and picked up on the cover of higher-latency weekly publications, it's already reflected in the price; the market is likely looking ahead to the next thing. Of course, this isn't a hard and fast rule.

That said, this fall The Economist has given us one and potentially two textbook examples of the magazine-cover indicator. Back in the first week of September, they published a cover story lauding NVIDIA (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang as "The Sorcerer of Silicon". While it didn't mark the exact top for the GPU giant, we all know what's happened since. The second leg of this potential contrarian two-fer was the cover story published in this week's issue. The story's title is "Why you should expect an AI crash" with cover art depicting cash and one unfortunate investor, tumbling into freefall below a stylized "AI" logo.

It remains to be seen whether the newest cover will mark the sentiment low for the AI trade. If it does, though, it wouldn't be the first time that a magazine cover focusing on a phenomenon marked a turning point in a trend. Either way, the latest AI cover story is one that will make contrarians everywhere sit up and say "huh"!

tweets.text:
When I get something wrong, I: 

-Make multiple videos saying I was wrong.
-Tweet multiple times saying I was wrong.
-Post multiple reasons for what I missed and how I can improve next time.

But when many others on this platform get something wrong, their first instinct is to lash out at those who are right or who disagree with them.

Instead of showing any self-reflection, maturity, or growth as a person/investor, they would rather go dunk on someone else who is not even bothering or thinking about them at all.

The entire crypto space is full of immature and emotional investors who have no ability to show accountability for anything.

If your first response to being wrong is "Let me go mock someone to make me feel better about myself" and not "Let me reflect on where I went wrong" then you are destined to make the same mistakes in the future.

What I got wrong is how high the Q3 bounce went (did not think it would take out the May high).

On the day of the low on July 1st, I said the accumulation zone had begun and to expect a relief rally. I was not calling for immediately lower at $57k. I actually said we would likely hold support there for a while.

Since you have been bull posting non-stop, why not take a few minutes to admit you were wrong over the last couple of months? Why not reflect on how you could be a better investor?

Why is your first instinct to lash out at someone that disagrees with you? 

Do I go to your page and mock you on all your bad calls?
